paragraphs.text: Tea Masters Cake is a cake of [ripe pu’er](shou:definition) made from Yunnan leaf. Before it was pressed, the leaf went through [wet piling](shou:wet-piling). It was wetted and heaped, then covered to hold in the heat its own microbes give off. Every week or so it was turned to spread that heat and let air in. The pile stays below about 65°C, because any hotter and the leaf starts to char.

The pile does in weeks what raw pu’er takes years of keeping to do, so a cake like this is ready to drink soon after it is made. Yunnan took up the method in 1973. That year a team from the Kunming, Menghai and Xiaguan factories went to [Guangzhou to learn its piling](shou:piling-1973), and by 1975 Menghai's way of doing it had become the ripe pu’er made today.

brewing.text: From a cake, brick or tuo, ease a piece off along the edge with a pick rather than snapping it. Whole leaves give up their flavour steadily; broken ones release it all at once and cloud the cup. Ripe pu’er takes boiling water: fermented, tightly packed leaf needs full heat to open, and it does not scald the way green tea can. A common start is about 7 grams to 100 ml and one quick rinse, which wakes the leaf and carries off dust and any pile smell. Then short steeps that lengthen as the leaf opens, so the cup stays clear rather than heavy; it gives eight or more good cups.

notice.text: A smooth, sweet cup with earthy or woody notes. A young ripe tea can carry a faint smell of the pile, which fades with airing or in the first steeps.
